title: Should You Move Your FD to SIP in 2026? The Honest Answer

summary: With the repo rate at 5.25% and FD returns dropping to 4 to 4.5% after tax, switching to SIP may make sense. Here's the framework, by time horizon.
primary_question: Should I move my fixed deposit money to a SIP when interest rates are falling?

content:
If your fixed deposit is paying 6 to 6.4% and you're in the 30% tax bracket, you keep roughly 4.2 to 4.5% after tax. India's retail inflation has run at 4 to 5% through 2026. So your FD is, at best, holding position. Not growing your money. The question isn't whether SIP is better in theory. It's whether the math actually justifies switching, and when.

Key Takeaways

  • SBI FDs pay up to 6.4% for general customers in 2026. After 30% income tax, you clear about 4.5%.
  • Don't break existing FDs. The early withdrawal penalty typically costs 0.5 to 1 percentage point off your rate.
  • The right decision point is maturity, not mid-tenure. Redirect money when the FD matures, not before.
  • For goals 5 years or further out, equity SIP has historically outrun FD returns. For under 3 years, FD is the safer call.
  • Keep 3 to 6 months of expenses in FD as a cushion, regardless of what the rest of your money does.

Why Your FD Returns Aren't What They Look Like

SBI pays up to 6.4% for standard retail FDs in 2026, with its Amrit Vrishti scheme at 6.45% for a 444-day tenure. That looks solid. But FD interest is taxed as regular income at your income slab rate. At 30%, a 6.4% FD becomes roughly 4.5% after tax. With inflation running at 4 to 5%, your real return is close to zero.

This is a pretty common situation, and definately worth examining before you auto-renew your next FD.

Say you have Rs 5 lakh in a one-year SBI FD at 6.4%. You earn Rs 32,000 in interest. Tax at 30% takes Rs 9,600. You keep Rs 22,400, which works out to about 4.5% net. That's right where inflation sits. You've preserved your money. You haven't grown it.

The 30% slab isn't everyone's situation. If you're in the 10% or 20% bracket, FDs do meaningfully better in real terms. That changes the calculation quite a bit.

Private banks offer higher rates. Bandhan Bank's 2 to 3 year FD pays 7.45% as of September 2026. But Bandhan is a smaller bank, and deposit insurance under DICGC covers only Rs 5 lakh per depositor. Worth knowing before you park a large sum there.

Should You Break Your FD Early to Start a SIP?

No, almost always not. Breaking an FD early typically costs you 0.5 to 1 percentage point below your contracted rate, and you lose some accumulated interest in the process. In most cases the penalty wipes out any benefit from moving sooner. Redirect new money at maturity instead. That's where the actual decision lives.

Banks handle early withdrawal penalties differently, but the structure is consistent across most of them. You get the rate for the tenure you actually held, minus a penalty of usually 0.5% to 1%. So if you locked in at 6.4% and break it at 8 months, you might receive closer to 5.5% for that period. Worth it? Rarely.

Most people think about these as two seperate questions when they're really part of the same decision. Should I break my FD? Probably not. What do I do when it matures? That's the real question, and the answer depends entirely on when you need the money.

FD vs SIP by Time Horizon

Time HorizonBetter OptionWhy
Under 2 yearsFDShort-term equity returns are volatile; capital safety matters more
2 to 3 yearsFD or balanced fundEquity needs more time to smooth out market swings
3 to 5 yearsSplit: part FD, part SIPGrowing horizon; start building equity exposure gradually
5 to 7 yearsSIP (equity)Market cycles tend to reward patient investors at this range
Over 7 yearsSIP, stronglyLong-run equity data shows negative return outcomes become rare past 7 years

How Much Should You Always Keep in FD?

Keep 3 to 6 months of your take-home pay in a liquid, safe instrument. An FD qualifies. A liquid mutual fund also works, though it carries minimal market risk. This buffer should not go into equity SIPs, regardless of how attractive the returns look. Emergency money needs to be accessible in days, not across market cycles.

This is where a lot of people get tripped up. They move all their FD money into SIP after reading that equity beats FD over 10 years, then need emergency funds 14 months later and redeem at exactly the wrong time. The equity advantage disappears fast in that scenario.

The rule is straightforward: SIP with money you genuinely won't need for at least 5 years. FD for everything else, plus your buffer. These two instruments are not rivals. They solve different problems. Use both.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happens to FD rates if RBI cuts rates again?

When the RBI cuts the repo rate, banks tend to lower new FD rates over the following weeks. Your existing FD is not affected; it keeps earning the contracted rate. New FDs opened after a cut will offer less. The repo rate has held at 5.25% through 2026, but a cut before year-end remains possible, which makes locking in current rates sensible if you need FD security.

Is a SIP return guaranteed?

No. Equity SIP returns depend on market performance. Historically, large-cap equity funds in India have returned 10 to 13% annually over 7 to 10 year periods. But past performance doesn't guarantee future results. Any 2 to 3 year window can be flat or negative, which is exactly why time horizon matters so much in this decision.

Does SIP have a tax advantage over FD?

Yes. Long-term capital gains on equity mutual funds are taxed at 12.5% on gains above Rs 1.25 lakh per year. FD interest is taxed at your full income slab rate, up to 30%. For someone in the 30% bracket, that tax difference alone can add up to 1.5 to 2 percentage points of effective annual return.

What if my goal is 3 to 4 years away?

Consider splitting your investable amount. Keep 40 to 60% in FD for capital protection and put the rest into a balanced advantage fund or hybrid mutual fund via SIP. These carry less equity risk than pure large-cap funds and tend to do better than FDs over 3-plus years without the full downside exposure of pure equity.

Can I run an FD and a SIP at the same time?

Most people should. The practical answer isn't to pick one. Keep your emergency buffer in FD and build long-term wealth through SIP. Monthly SIP inflows in India hit Rs 30,954 crore in May 2026. Many of those investors still hold FDs, because the instruments serve different needs, not the same one.

The Short Version

Your FD is not beating inflation after tax if you're in the 30% bracket. But that doesn't mean you should break it. When it matures, decide based on when you'll actually need the money. Under 3 years, stay in FD. Over 5 years, SIP is the stronger call. Keep 3 to 6 months of expenses liquid, always. These instruments solve different problems. Use both.
